Photo by Dennis Schroeder, NLR 98941 22 https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2024.115070 Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 | 47 Improving Weather Modeling for Power System Planning Extreme weather, shifting demand patterns, and variable energy generation all challenge the reliability of the U.S. electric grid. DOE’s Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium (GMLC) brings together national laboratories to confront these pressures by enhancing the data and modeling capabilities that underpin grid planning. Within this consortium, the Energy System Planning for Resilience during Severe Weather project is transforming how weather data are incorporated into power system models. This work helps researchers and planners better understand and prepare for potential weather-driven impacts on the nation’s power system. This project uses HPC and AI to fuse weather data into a suite of energy planning and risk management tools. Using Kestrel, researchers developed and applied state-of-the-art generative ML methods to produce high- resolution weather scenarios, resulting in 400 years of weather data over the entire contiguous United States, to more fully capture possible future conditions and extremes. In parallel, the project is using an optimized Weather Research and Forecasting model configuration to produce physics-based dynamically downscaled meteorological datasets. Work from this project, including the development of the generative weather dataset, was featured in Data in Brief.23 Both datasets strengthen models used to evaluate future load, energy resource availability, and energy generation potential across a wide range of weather scenarios. Built and operated by NLR, the GDR preserves, curates, and delivers geothermal research data to the public—supporting scientific transparency, reducing duplication, and accelerating research efforts across the geothermal community. Hosted on NLR’s cloud computing infrastructure, the GDR provides the scalable, reliable foundation needed to support open access to large, growing datasets. A new AI-powered research assistant called AskGDR further improves how users discover and use this free data. With more than 1,300 datasets, 760 terabytes of data, and 28 million downloads, the GDR is one of the largest and most widely used geothermal data resources in the world.
